name: Animation from Interactions
explanation: When a user interaction, like scrolling, hovering, or clicking, triggers a motion animation such as a parallax effect or an element sliding, zooming, or spinning into view, there needs to be a way to turn that animation off. The exception is when the motion itself is essential to what's being communicated or to the function of the feature, such as a video editing timeline where the animation is the actual content, not a decorative effect layered on top of it.
whoItAffects: People with vestibular disorders can experience dizziness, nausea, or headaches triggered by motion effects like parallax scrolling or large zoom/slide transitions, even when the motion isn't a rapid flash. People with attention-related disabilities can find animated transitions distracting or disorienting when they occur frequently as a side effect of ordinary interactions like scrolling. Providing a setting to disable interaction-triggered animation lets these users browse comfortably without losing access to the underlying content or functionality.
howToTest: Interact with the page the way a typical user would: scroll through it, hover over elements, click buttons and links. Note any motion effects that trigger as a result, parallax backgrounds, sliding panels, zooming images, animated transitions. Then enable your operating system's reduce-motion setting and repeat the same interactions; the animations should be significantly reduced or removed, unless that specific motion is essential to understanding the content or completing the task.

check.question: A marketing site uses a parallax scrolling effect where background images move at a different speed than foreground text as the user scrolls, purely for visual style. The site does not respect the operating system's reduced-motion setting and offers no other way to disable it. Does this pass SC 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions?
choices: Yes, because parallax scrolling is a common design trend
No, because the interaction-triggered animation isn't essential to the content and there's no way to disable it
Yes, because the effect only involves background images, not interactive controls
It depends only on how fast the user scrolls
